summary: Specifies a packet format that can carry multiple messages, for use by routing protocols in mobile ad hoc networks. This is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 7631 and RFC 8245.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5444 defines a common way for mobile ad hoc routing protocols to package messages and addresses. Its compact, extensible format lets one packet carry multiple messages.

questions: what is an address block in manet
subtitle: A shared packet structure for carrying messages used by mobile ad hoc routing protocols.

tldr.problem: Mobile ad hoc routing protocols need a compact way to send messages and address information over links that may have limited capacity. Different protocols also need a format that can be extended without losing the ability to parse older content.
tldr.mechanism: A packet carries a header and zero or more messages. Messages contain headers, address blocks that compress shared address parts, and type-length-value attributes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5444 defines syntax rather than a routing protocol. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 7631 and RFC 8245.

today: RFC 5444 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7631 and RFC 8245. It has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: A Shared Format for MANET Messages
sections.content:
RFC 5444 defines the syntax of packets that can carry routing-protocol messages between Mobile Ad hoc NETwork (MANET) routers. It defines a format, not a routing protocol; different MANET protocols can use it.

The format supports generic parsing, extension with new messages and attributes, compact representation of shared address parts, and forwarding decisions based on message-header information without reading the full message body.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines how to package routing messages, not how routers choose routes. Different MANET protocols can use the same packet structure.

sections.title: Packets and Messages
sections.content:
A packet begins with a header and can contain zero or more messages. The header includes a 4-bit version, a 4-bit flags field, and optional packet sequence number and TLV block. The network layer supplies the packet length, so the packet format does not repeat it.

Each message has a header, a message-level TLV block and zero or more address blocks followed by address-block TLV blocks. Its fixed header includes an 8-bit message type, 4 flag bits, a 4-bit address-length value and a 16-bit message size. The address-length value is the address size in octets minus 1: 3 for IPv4 and 15 for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet is a container for messages. Each message has a header and can carry address lists and attributes.

sections.title: Compact Address Blocks
sections.content:
An Address Block can describe one or more addresses or address prefixes. Each address is represented as Head, Mid and Tail: addresses in the block share the same Head and Tail, while each has its own Mid. A zero-filled Tail can be signaled without sending those octets.

The block states how many addresses it contains and which optional fields follow. It can include one prefix length for all addresses or a separate prefix length for each one. A prefix length longer than the address itself makes the block malformed.
sections.plainLanguage: An address block can write shared beginning and ending parts once. It then lists the different middle parts and any prefix lengths.

sections.title: TLVs Carry Attributes
sections.content:
A type-length-value (TLV) attaches an attribute to a packet, message or address. Its type identifies the attribute, its length says how much data follows, and its value contains that data. A parser can skip an attribute type it does not understand.

TLVs are grouped in blocks. An address-block TLV can apply to one address, a continuous range or every address in the block; its value can be shared or supplied once per address. Each protocol using this format must define how to handle conflicting attributes and the order in which to process them.
sections.plainLanguage: A TLV labels an attribute, gives its length and carries its value. Unknown TLVs can be skipped, while the routing protocol defines how known attributes work.

sections.title: Discarding Malformed Elements
sections.content:
An element is malformed if it cannot be parsed according to the format, including when too few octets are available. A malformed element in the packet header means the whole packet must be silently discarded.

If a malformed element occurs within a message, that message must be silently discarded. A receiver must not process or forward the malformed packet or message.
sections.plainLanguage: If a receiver cannot parse a packet header, it discards the packet. If only one message is malformed, it discards that message.

sections.title: Multiplexing and Scoped Forwarding
sections.content:
A packet can carry messages from different protocols, so a multiplexing and demultiplexing process must direct each message to its owning protocol or silently discard it. This allows several messages to share one packet.

The format can also support scope-limited flooding. A protocol can identify messages by originator address, sequence number and message type, then reduce the hop limit and increase the hop count when forwarding. The message should be discarded when its hop limit reaches zero or its hop count reaches 255.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver sends each message to the protocol that owns its type. Hop fields can limit how far a message travels through the network.

sections.title: Security Depends on the Using Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 5444 defines a packet format rather than a protocol, so it does not require a security mechanism. A protocol using it can add end-to-end authentication with a signature in a message TLV, or hop-by-hop authentication with a signature in a packet TLV.

Confidentiality is normally provided by link-layer or IP-layer mechanisms. A protocol can also define encrypted TLV values, but it must specify the encrypted data format and encryption mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet format does not provide security by itself. A protocol using it can define signatures or encryption for its messages.
